newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan insurers in no rush to sell dollars for yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan insurers in no rush to sell dollars for yen.

text.p: Life insurance firms, Japan's biggest holders of foreign securities, are in no rush to sell off dollars, officials at insurers said on Monday.
In fact, some now see the dollar as a bargain buy after its steep falls, they said.

Japanese trust banks and securities houses have already dumped dollars actively to hedge their foreign assets against risks of it tumbling, the main factor behind its dive by more than six yen since Friday.
Currency dealers have been wondering if life insurers will follow suit.

"There's no change in our foreign investment stance. We are not considering using currency hedging," said Masanori Mizoguchi, general manager of the securities investment department at Nippon Dantai Life Insurance Co Ltd.
"Instead, we see the current levels as good (to bargain-hunt for dollars)."
The dollar has taken a nearly 10 yen dive in just seven trading days from its recent peak and traded as low as 117.50 yen on Monday. It stood at around 118.50 yen in later-afternoon trade in Tokyo.
"The recent talking down of the dollar might have a greater impact than they (Finance Ministry officials) have thought," Mizoguchi added.
On Monday, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, in an apparent effort to put a brake on the dollar's slide, told reporters that the dollar was likely to settle down soon.
Taku Yamasaki, the policy research chief of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), said on Monday that a dollar/yen exchange rate of around 120 yen would be the most appropriate.
Japan's cash-rich life insurers held around 17.10 trillion yen in foreign securities at the end of February this year.
They have generally kept the foreign securities without currency hedging, and even one percent hedging could cause a substantial amount of dollar sales.

An official at the nation's largest insurer, Nippon Life Insurance Co, said there had been no major change in its stance towards overseas investments since the fundamental picture had not altered. He said the firm plans to purchase about 300 billion yen in foreign securities in the current fiscal year.

Akira Yutani, manager of the separate account planning division at Dai-Ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co, said the division had not started using currency hedging in foreign bond and stock investments, which amount to 22 percent of its accounts.
"Separate" or special accounts at life insurers offer the chance of greater returns but have greater exposure to foreign asset risks than general accounts.
"It necessary to watch closely to see if the dollar will fall below 115 yen," Yutani said.
Taisuke Tanaka, a strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston in Tokyo, said: "It is unrealistic to imagine insurers will rush to start hedging, even if it starts falling below 115 yen."
"But such sales may emerge when the dollar recovers to 120 yen."
Worries over Japan's rising trade surplus with the United States have flared up, helping to drag the dollar down against the yen, currency dealers said.

Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus for April, due to be announced next Monday, is expected to total 809.9 billion yen, up 156.9 percent from 315.3 billion yen a year earlier, private research company Daiwa Bank Research Institute said on Monday.
